newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: ALPINE SKIING-UNHAPPY RACERS NOT WALKING SO TALL.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-UNHAPPY RACERS NOT WALKING SO TALL.

text.p: Alpine ski racers are not walking so tall this season and some of them are not happy.
As a safety measure, the size of plates under the boot has been cut to restrict the distance between the bottom of the ski and the top of the binding to six cms (2.35 in).

Next season it will be dropped to 5.5 cms (2.15 in). Over the last three years, some had risen as high as 15 cms (5.9 in) as ski companies discovered that a greater height combined with new style skis -- wide at the top and narrower at the centre -- made for faster cornering.

But ski racing's ruling body, the FIS, has concluded the combination is too risky and suggested it might even have contributed to the tragic death on 1994 of double world champion Ulrike Maier of Austria.

FIS president Marc Hodler said accidents had started occurring on relatively flat parts of the slope when a racer was going straight and suddenly lost control of his or her ski -- and that this may have been caused by extremely high plates.
"It could have been the case in a very bad women's accident some years ago, although we cannot be certain," Hodler said in a clear reference to Maier's death.
Maier was killed from neck injuries sustained in a fall during a World Cup downhill at Garmisch-Partenkirchen, Germany.
Professor Werner Nachbauer, who has carried out studies for the FIS at the University of Innsbruck, said the ski federation was right to introduce such measures.

"Try walking down a steep mountain with high-heeled shoes. You have less control and stability. It is similar to the effect of an extremely high plate on a ski," he said. "The larger the distance between the foot and the ski, the easier it is for a skier to lose control of his skis."
Nachbauer said high plates also put more strain on the knees and could have been the cause of the numerous knee injuries in ski racing lately.
"We encourage young people to get into ski racing and then it is so dangerous that their bodies can often not deal with the strain," he said.

However, several Austrian skiers including Olympic and world downhill champion Patrick Ortlieb, argue that low plates increase the chances of the ski boot coming to contact with the snow in corners which in turn increase the chances of a fall.

But Nachbauer felt six cms was enough to avoid the problem and said: "What is important is to avoid the extreme. We cannot allow a skier to stand 100 to 150 mms (10-15 cms) above the snow -- this was already happening in some cases."

Ski veteran and winner of the women's 1993 overall World Cup, Anita Wachter said: "High plates do cause more injuries but it is also dangerous if the ski boot touches the snow. However, ski racing is dangerous and we are all aware of this."
Wachter said skiers had agreed to the six cms but they would not accept the reduction to 5.5 cms. "This is not fair on ski companies who have worked in this direction," she said.

Guenther Hujara, FIS chief race director, said: "The question we asked ourselves was: 'should we allow commercial interests to take priority until the next major accident occurs?' We answered this question with a clear 'no.'"
"We are not killing the sport; there are limits and regulations in all sports."
A new ski currently on the market can only be used to its full effect if the height of the boot above the snow is raised to a certain level.
Hujara acknowledged: "If we set height limits in ski racing then this obviously has counter-effects on the marketing concepts of these ski companies."
But he added:"We are not responsible for the consumer market, we are a competition organisation."

Professor Nachbauer felt the new skis were not dangerous for the average enthusiast because they did not reach racing speed. But he added: "We will see throughout the course of the winter. It's too early to say now."

Hujara deflected claims that the FIS had not consulted the racers before bringing in the new rule. "If we commission an investigation and the facts are clear they we simply have to do something to protect the skiers from themselves," he said.
The Alpine ski World Cup season moved into gear this weekend with the action centred on Park City, Utah.
The opening race, a women's giant slalom, went to Italy's Sabina Panzanini with Wachter in second.
